title: Tisha B'Av
hook: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting on the floor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot: a night awake for the gift of the Torah, and Ruth's great promise. Your line was stay up for the gift. Today, the last stop on our walk through the year, and a day of mourning. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

One word, chanted slowly in a dim room: eichah. How. It's the first word of the book of Lamentations, and in Hebrew it's also the book's name. On this summer night the curtain has been taken off the ark. People aren't in their seats; they're sitting on the floor, or on low stools, some in socks or canvas sneakers. No one greets anyone with a hello. The reader goes on by a small light, verse after verse. The whole room sits low, as if someone has died. In a way, someone has.
screen: `ONE WORD: EICHAH. HOW.` → `THE CURTAIN OFF THE ARK.` → `SITTING ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Tisha B'Av means the ninth of the month of Av. It's a day of mourning. On this date, the Mishnah says, both Temples in Jerusalem were destroyed: the first by Babylon, and the second by Rome. The Mishnah adds other sorrows to the same date, and over the centuries, later tragedies were remembered on it too, among them, by later tradition, the expulsion of the Jews from Spain. So Tisha B'Av became the day to mourn many losses at once. It's kept like a day of mourning for a close relative. A fast, from sunset to nightfall, like Yom Kippur, but it gives way to health: anyone ill, pregnant, nursing or at risk asks a doctor and a rabbi. No leather shoes. No washing for pleasure. And people sit on the floor or low stools, the way mourners do in the week after a funeral. Then the book of Lamentations is read, five short poems of grief over Jerusalem. It opens: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" Even Torah study, usually a joy, is limited to sad texts. Still, the day isn't only despair. The rabbis asked why the Second Temple fell, and answered: baseless hatred, people hating each other for nothing. So the day becomes a call to repair how people treat each other. At midday, mourners may rise from the floor. And there's an old tradition that on Tisha B'Av, of all days, the redeemer is born. And near its end, Lamentations pleads to begin again: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." When the book is read aloud, that verse is said again after the last one, so the reading ends on it. And that closes our walk through the year: the calendar and the moon, the new year and the fast, the booth, the lights, the trees, the scroll, the seder, the count, the gift, and today, the floor.
screen: `TISHA B'AV: THE NINTH OF AV.` · `BOTH TEMPLES, AND LATER SORROWS.` · `SITTING LOW, LIKE A MOURNER.` · `BASELESS HATRED, AND A HOPE.` · then, large: `RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit on the floor for five minutes. You can start now. If it's comfortable for you, lower yourself to the floor; if not, sit low in a chair. Settle, and breathe. Think of one loss you carry, big or small. You don't have to fix it or explain it. Just let the ground hold you while you hold it. If you pray, you can say the old line from Lamentations: renew our days. The bell holds the time.
Tisha B'Av. The ninth of Av: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting low.
Your line: the floor holds grief. When something is heavy today, sit down low for a minute, and let the ground take some of the weight. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations and mournful poems (kinot) chanted in dim light.

what a scholar hears: Mishnah Taanit 4:6 lists five calamities on the ninth of Av; Yoma 9b on baseless hatred; the redeemer born on Tisha B'Av in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4.

notes: Added 2026-10-06 from the five-year map (standing rule: every fast-day lesson carries the health line; never present fasting as required at risk to health): one sentence that health and life come first. Minor fasts (Tenth of Tevet, Fast of Esther, Seventeenth of Tammuz): the ill, pregnant and nursing are generally excused (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 550:1 and 686:2 with commentaries). Tisha B'Av: the ill and anyone at risk eat; others ask a doctor and a rabbi (OC 554:5-6). Confirm with the Keeper.
Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Lamentations 1:1 and 5:21.

First Temple destroyed 586 BCE (some date 587); 'about two thousand six hundred years ago'. Second Temple 70 CE. The Bible dates the first destruction to the 7th/10th of Av; tradition fixes the fast on the 9th (Taanit 29a).
Expulsion from Spain linked to Tisha B'Av by later tradition (the edict's deadline fell near it). Confirm phrasing.
The practice line 'renew our days' is quoted from Lamentations as optional for those who pray; not a new prayer.
End of the 'holidays as they arrive' section (days 121–138): look-back list in the teach.
